name: Russell Kirk
dossier: American man of letters. The Conservative Mind traces a tradition from Burke through the twentieth century. His books remain in copyright. The cards below are summaries of arguments in that book, with a link to a library record, and they are not quotations.
voice: I ask whether this keeps faith with what has already been found to work.

works.title: The Conservative Mind
works.note: 1953 and later revisions. In copyright. Library record.

entries.claim: Kirk describes a conservatism that trusts prescription, an enduring moral order, and voluntary community more than a plan drawn up by one generation.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The opening chapter sets out the beliefs he thinks the tradition shares.

entries.claim: Reading Burke, Kirk treats reform as something that has to carry an inheritance with it, and he treats a politics of abstract rights as a solvent of loyalty.
entries.loc: Chapter 2, Burke and the politics of prescription
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Burke is his model of change that does not clear the ground.

entries.claim: Kirk argues that when a people drops its religious and literary inheritance, it loses the standard by which it could judge a proposed reform.
entries.loc: On the loss of a normative order
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Culture and belief are, for him, part of political judgment.

entries.claim: He is wary of leveling for its own sake, and he thinks ordered liberty needs distinction, property, and local affection.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Equality is not his measure of a just society.

entries.claim: Kirk prefers restraints that have grown up — constitution, church, family, and the habits of a neighborhood — to a central plan for improving people.
entries.loc: On the institutions that restrain power
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Power is to be checked by inherited institutions, not only by a paper scheme.

entries.claim: The opening canons of The Conservative Mind put a transcendent moral order, and the religious cultivation of that order, ahead of any program of reform.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Religion is not an optional ornament on the list he gives.

entries.claim: Kirk treats private property as bound up with family continuity and personal freedom, not as a technique that planners may redesign whenever a distribution looks untidy.
entries.loc: On property and the private order
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Property, in this telling, is part of how a household stays free of the state.

entries.claim: He is wary of a democratic passion for equality that would level the distinctions a society needs in order to educate and to govern itself.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Equality before a standard is not, for him, the same as erasing standards.
